note: English player text for the wine bar's rockets (ORDER 273, Vision Owner 2026-09-28: the game is in English). Written by Claude Code from the Swedish drafts, which are kept in vinbar.text.sv.draft.json. Placeholders: {bord} (table), {gäst} (guest), {vin} (wine), {personal} (staff), {klockan} (the time in game time); the code fills them.

vb01-korken.title: The first bottle
vb01-korken.body: The evening's first bottle: {gäst} at table {bord} has ordered a {vin}. When {personal} draws the cork, it smells of damp cellar and wet cardboard.

guestLine.a: “There's nothing wrong, is there? We've been looking forward to this wine all week.”
guestLine.b: “You smelled the cork for a long time. Is everything all right? It's our favourite wine.”

steps.question: What does a smell of damp cellar and wet cardboard tell you?

a.label: Reduction, that is sulphur compounds
a.explanation: Reduction smells of struck match or sulphur and can often be aired away. Damp cellar is something else.

b.label: Oxidation, too much oxygen
b.explanation: Oxidised wine smells of tired apple, nuts or sherry. Cellar and cardboard point to the cork.

c.label: Cork taint, the compound TCA
c.explanation: The smell comes from the compound TCA. The fault is in that particular bottle, not in the wine as such.

d.label: A young, closed wine that needs air
d.explanation: A young wine can say little, but it does not smell of cellar. The smell is a fault, not an age.

fail.outcome: {personal} puts the bottle on the table without knowing what is wrong. The guest waits.

steps.clue: Analysis: The fault is in the cork.

steps.question: What is the guest looking for?

a.label: To be spared hearing about problems
a.explanation: The guest asked straight out. Someone who asks wants an answer.

b.label: That very wine, and an honest answer
b.explanation: The guest wants the wine they chose, and to know what is happening.

c.label: Something nice to start with, anything at all really
c.explanation: The guest wants to get going, but chose that very wine.

fail.outcome: The guest looks at the bill and then at {personal}. The mood at the table cools.

steps.clue: Experience: The guest asked straight out.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Say it is corked, open a new bottle and change glasses.
a.explanation: A corked bottle is always replaced, and the glasses too, since the smell lingers. Cork taint is no shame. Saying so openly builds trust.

b.label: Open a new bottle, change the glasses and say nothing about the fault.
b.explanation: The bottle and glasses are changed correctly. But the guest asked, and silence looks as if the bar is hiding something.

c.label: Say honestly that the wine is closed and decant it at the table.
c.explanation: The honesty is right, but air helps against reduction, not cork taint. TCA does not go away with oxygen.

d.label: Serve it anyway and say the smell belongs to the wine's character.
d.explanation: Cork taint is a fault in the bottle. The guest notices, and trust in the whole wine list falls.

fail.outcome: The guest tastes, frowns and puts the glass down.
fail.ongoing: The guest at table {bord} sits with an untouched glass and looks around for the staff.

fail.outcome: The decanter stands on the table. The smell is still there.
fail.ongoing: The decanter stands on the table. The smell of cellar is still there.

halfGrip.analysis: The bottle was replaced correctly, but the guest got no answer to their question.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: The new bottle is on the table, but the guest still looks puzzled.
halfGrip.experience: The answer was honest, but cork taint cannot be aired away. Only a new bottle helps.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: The decanter is on the table. The guest tastes and wrinkles their nose.

success.outcome: A new bottle and new glasses. The guest nods after the first taste.

staff.outcome: The bottle is served as it is, and the guest sends it back after the first glass.

staffTexts.success: Sara recognises the cork and replaces the bottle without saying much.
staffTexts.fail: The bottle is served as it is, and the guest sends it back after the first glass.

vb02-rosen.title: The rosé's temperature
vb02-rosen.body: The evening is warm. The whites are at 10 degrees in the fridge, but the rosés that just arrived are at 24 degrees. The first guests want rosé.

guestLine.a: “Something cold and fresh, rosé if you have it. We've walked in the sun all day.”
guestLine.b: “We've cycled all the way from Hjulsjö. Have you got rosé, really cold?”

steps.question: At what temperature should a rosé be served?

a.label: Room temperature, around 22 degrees
a.explanation: That warm, the rosé tastes heavy and sweet, and the alcohol sticks out.

b.label: 16–18 degrees, like a red
b.explanation: That suits many reds. A rosé needs to be colder for its freshness to show.

c.label: Ice cold, 2–4 degrees
c.explanation: Too cold closes the nose, and the wine tastes of almost nothing.

d.label: 8–10 degrees
d.explanation: Then the rosé is fresh without the nose disappearing.

fail.outcome: {personal} pours a glass of rosé from the shelf. It tastes lukewarm.

steps.clue: Analysis: The bottles are too warm.

steps.question: What are the guests looking for?

a.label: Rosé, and the temperature matters less
a.explanation: They said cold first. They will remember a lukewarm rosé on a warm evening.

b.label: Something to drink quickly, anything
b.explanation: It is urgent, but they asked for rosé.

c.label: Cooling down now, and a cold rosé
c.explanation: Two wishes: something cold straight away, and the rosé they asked for.

fail.outcome: The guests at the bar exchange looks. Some order beer instead.

steps.clue: Experience: The guests are hot and thirsty.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Bottles in ice water, say “ten minutes”, offer cold water.
a.explanation: Ice and water chill a bottle in ten to fifteen minutes, much faster than the fridge. The guests know why it takes time and have something cold in hand.

b.label: Serve the rosé now, with ice cubes in the glass to cool it.
b.explanation: The guests get something cold straight away, but the ice dilutes the wine and takes away both nose and acidity.

c.label: Bottles in ice and water, and take the order meanwhile.
c.explanation: The chilling is right, but the guests stand empty-handed and don't know why it takes time.

d.label: Serve the warm rosé as it is and hope nobody notices.
d.explanation: The guests notice at the first sip.

fail.outcome: The ice cubes clink. After a while the wine tastes of water.
fail.ongoing: The rosé glasses stand half full on the tables. The guests order nothing more.

fail.outcome: The ice cubes clink. After a while the wine tastes of water.
fail.ongoing: The rosé glasses stand half full on the tables. The guests order nothing more.

halfGrip.analysis: The rosé got cold, but the guests stood with nothing in hand and no word why.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: The guests wait at the bar and look at the clock.
halfGrip.experience: They got something cold at once, but the ice dilutes the rosé. It is the bottle that should be chilled.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: The ice cubes clink. After a while the wine tastes of water.

success.outcome: The buckets stand on the bar. The first rosé glasses are cold and misted.

staff.outcome: The rosé is served as it is. It tastes warm and sweet.

staffTexts.success: Per puts the bottles on ice and pours water meanwhile.
staffTexts.fail: The rosé is served as it is. It tastes warm and sweet.

vb03-notallergi.title: Nut allergy
vb03-notallergi.body: {gäst} at table {bord} has a nut allergy and asks whether the bruschetta with basil pesto is all right. {personal} is unsure what is in the pesto.

guestLine.a: “I don't usually dare order anything with a sauce when I eat out. Tonight I just want to eat without worrying.”
guestLine.b: “Last time I ate out I ended up in hospital. I just want an ordinary evening.”

steps.question: What is in a classic basil pesto?

a.label: Basil, pine nuts, garlic, hard cheese and olive oil
a.explanation: Pine nuts are seeds and are not among the nuts that must be labelled under EU rules, but many people with a nut allergy react to them. The hard cheese contains milk, which is also an allergen. Tonight's recipe must still be checked.

b.label: Basil, peanuts and oil
b.explanation: Peanuts are not part of classic pesto.

c.label: Basil, hazelnuts and cheese
c.explanation: The nut in the original is the pine nut.

d.label: Only basil, cheese and oil
d.explanation: A common mistake. Classic pesto contains pine nuts.

fail.outcome: {personal} stays at the table without an answer. The guest waits for a reply.

steps.clue: Analysis: The pesto may contain something the guest reacts to.

steps.question: What is the guest looking for?

a.label: To avoid the pesto
a.explanation: That is part of it, but the guest wants to eat without worry all evening.

b.label: To be reassured that it will probably be fine
b.explanation: “Probably” is exactly what makes the guest worried.

c.label: A sure answer and a dish without worry
c.explanation: The guest needs facts and an evening without worry, and both require that the kitchen knows.

fail.outcome: The guest gets a different dish, but the kitchen knows nothing about the allergy.

steps.clue: Experience: The guest is afraid and wants to be able to relax.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Ask the kitchen, answer plainly, suggest a safe dish, mark the order.
a.explanation: An allergy answer rests on the recipe and the kitchen. Once the order is marked, it is kept free of nuts all the way to the table.

b.label: Ask the kitchen, say what the pesto contains and let the guest choose.
b.explanation: The answer is right, but the guest is left alone with the worry before the next dish.

c.label: Advise against the bruschetta and suggest another dish, without asking the kitchen.
c.explanation: The guest feels looked after, but nobody knows what is in the new dish.

d.label: Say there are probably no nuts in the pesto, so it should be fine.
d.explanation: Guessing about allergens is the most dangerous mistake in service. The guest must get correct allergen information.

fail.outcome: The bruschetta goes out with traces of pesto left on the bread.
The bruschetta goes out to the table.
fail.ongoing: The bruschetta is on the table. Nobody knows what is in the pesto.

halfGrip.analysis: The answer was right, but the guest had to search alone and is still worried.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: The guest reads the menu for a long time and orders only bread.
halfGrip.experience: The guest felt looked after, but nobody asked the kitchen and the order is not marked.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: The dish goes out. The kitchen knows nothing about the allergy.

success.outcome: The guest gets a dish the kitchen has confirmed, and thanks you for taking the question seriously.

staff.outcome: The staff answer at random and serve the bruschetta.

staffTexts.success: Elin goes to the kitchen, checks the recipe and marks the order.
staffTexts.fail: The staff answer at random and serve the bruschetta.

vb04-dubbelbokning.title: The same table twice
vb04-dubbelbokning.body: Two parties stand at the door with a booking for table {bord}, at the same time. Both have received a confirmation.

guestLine.a: One party: “We booked in May, it's Mum's seventieth.” The other: “We have a confirmation too, we've driven from Örebro.”
guestLine.b: One party: “We've looked forward to this for months.” The other: “We only have two hours before our train.”

steps.question: What is a confirmed booking to the guest?

a.label: A request that the restaurant can change
a.explanation: Once the restaurant has confirmed, it is no longer a request. The guest has planned the evening around the answer.

b.label: A promise of a table at a certain time
b.explanation: A confirmation is the restaurant's promise. Both parties have such a promise, so the mistake is the restaurant's and the restaurant must solve it.

c.label: Valid only if the guest has paid a deposit
c.explanation: A deposit protects against no-shows. It is not what makes a booking valid. The confirmation is enough.

d.label: Valid only if the guest calls to confirm the table on the same day
d.explanation: Some restaurants ask guests to confirm again, but without such a rule the confirmation stands as it is.

fail.outcome: {personal} says it will probably work out. Both parties look doubtful.

steps.clue: Analysis: Both have a promise. The mistake is the restaurant's.

steps.question: What do the two parties need?

a.label: An apology, and that you take time to sort out the mistake
a.explanation: The apology is right, but the inquiry can wait until after the evening.

b.label: That the most important evening comes first
b.explanation: Both evenings matter to the people having them. It is not for the restaurant to judge.

c.label: A quick and fair answer for both
c.explanation: Both stand at the door with a promise, and both need to know now.

fail.outcome: Both parties are still standing in the entrance. The queue grows behind them.
fail.ongoing: The entrance is full of waiting guests. The staff walk back and forth with the phone.

steps.clue: Experience: Both are waiting at the door and need an answer now.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Check the system for who booked first, and ask the others to come back later on.
a.explanation: The book decides correctly, but the other party is sent away with nothing.

b.label: Give the table to the celebration, and the others a glass at the bar.
b.explanation: Thoughtful, but the book should decide, not whose evening seems most important.

c.label: Let both wait while you ring round to find out whose mistake it was.
c.explanation: The guests at the door need a decision now, and a crowded entrance shows across the whole room.

d.label: Check the system for who booked first. The others get the bar and a glass.
d.explanation: The book decides, and whoever has to wait gets something for the trouble. A glass costs little and turns a mistake into a good story.

fail.outcome: The parties stand comparing their confirmations. Nobody knows who is right.

halfGrip.analysis: The book decided correctly, but the other party left with nothing.
halfGrip.experience: The thought was right, but the table was promised to those who booked first.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: The other party leaves. One of them types something on their phone.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: The party that booked first watches the others sit down.

success.outcome: One party sits down. The other gets glasses at the bar and raises a toast.

staff.outcome: The staff let both wait, and one of the parties left.

staffTexts.success: Per checks the system, gives the table to those who booked first and treats the others at the bar.
staffTexts.fail: The staff let both wait, and one of the parties left.

vb05-dj.title: The music
vb05-dj.body: It is {klockan} and the DJ has turned the volume up. A couple at table {bord} lean across the table to hear each other.

guestLine.a: The woman at the table: “We haven't seen each other in ages. We want to be able to talk.”
guestLine.b: The man at the table, quietly: “It's our first date. I can't hear what she's saying.”

steps.question: What do guests do when the music gets louder?

a.label: Raise their voices, so the room gets even louder
a.explanation: We speak louder the more noise there is around us. This is called the Lombard effect. That is why the noise level in a room rises faster than the music is turned up.

b.label: Get used to it and hear each other better after a while
b.explanation: The ear does not adjust so that speech becomes clearer. Instead, the guests get tired and talk less.

c.label: Nothing, if the music has no vocals
c.explanation: Even music without vocals drowns out speech. Vocals disturb more, but the volume is what decides.

fail.outcome: {personal} shrugs. The couple keep leaning across the table.

steps.clue: Analysis: Louder music makes the whole room louder.

steps.question: What are the guests looking for?

a.label: To be able to talk, without having to move or leave
a.explanation: They came for the conversation. It is the music that should adapt, not them.

b.label: A table further away from the music
b.explanation: It helps them, but not the room, and not the next couple who sit down.

c.label: That the music is switched off completely, for the rest of the evening
c.explanation: They asked to hear each other, not for silence. Later in the evening the room needs the music.

fail.outcome: The couple finish their drinks and leave. Another table asks for the bill.
fail.ongoing: The couple at the table sit in silence and look at the clock.

steps.clue: Experience: The guests want to talk, and the room is still half empty.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Move the couple to the far end, away from the speakers.
a.explanation: The couple can talk, but the room stays just as loud, and the next couple meets the same thing.

b.label: Let the music play, it is part of the concept.
b.explanation: In a half-empty room early in the evening the music disturbs more than it carries.

c.label: Talk to the couple at the table, and ask the DJ to lower it until the room fills.
c.explanation: At the table you hear what the guests hear. A lower volume breaks the spiral where everyone talks louder, and it can go up again when the room wants to dance.

d.label: Ask the DJ to turn it down a little, and go back and check again in half an hour.
d.explanation: The right step for the room, but the couple get no help now and don't know you have noticed.

fail.outcome: {personal} thinks it sounds fine from the bar. At the table nothing can be heard.

halfGrip.analysis: The volume came down, but the couple got no help in the moment.
halfGrip.experience: The couple can talk, but the room is just as loud for everyone else.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: The couple finish their drinks before the music is lowered.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: The next couple by the speakers lean across the table.

success.outcome: The couple are talking again, and the room has the sound level the evening needs.

staff.outcome: Nobody said anything to the DJ. Two tables left early.

staffTexts.success: Sara asks the couple and asks the DJ to turn it down.
staffTexts.fail: Nobody said anything to the DJ. Two tables left early.

vb06-kylen.title: The fridge shows nine degrees
vb06-kylen.body: At the evening's first food safety check, the fridge with cheese and charcuterie shows 9 degrees.

guestLine.a: The chef: “We have twenty booked tonight, and the cheese board is what we sell most.”
guestLine.b: Sara: “Should I keep plating charcuterie, or what?”

steps.question: What do nine degrees in the fridge mean for cheese and charcuterie?

a.label: Within the margin, the fridge will recover
a.explanation: A fridge that is above the limit rarely gets better on its own. Without action and records, the restaurant has no defence if the food goes bad.

b.label: The food is spoiled and must all be thrown away at once
b.explanation: Safe, but needlessly expensive. Food that has been at 9 degrees for a short time can be moved and assessed.

c.label: Above the limit, a deviation that requires action
c.explanation: Chilled food must be kept at 8 degrees at most, preferably around 4. Nine degrees is a deviation that must be dealt with and written into the food safety check records.

fail.outcome: The fridge hums. The thermometer still shows nine.
fail.ongoing: The fridge hums. The thermometer still shows nine degrees.

steps.clue: Analysis: Nine degrees is a deviation to be dealt with and written down.

steps.question: What does the evening need?

a.label: That the team knows where things stand, and the evening can still go on
a.explanation: Everyone working tonight needs the same picture, otherwise someone opens the broken fridge again.

b.label: That the cheese board and the charcuterie come off completely tonight
b.explanation: Safe, but it costs the evening's best sellers for no reason.

c.label: That nobody needs to bother, it's already sorted
c.explanation: Nobody knows where the goods are, or what can be sold.

fail.outcome: {personal} looks for the charcuterie in the wrong fridge in the middle of service.

steps.clue: Experience: The team needs to know where things stand.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Measure in the food, move it to the other fridge, log the deviation and tell the team.
a.explanation: The measurement shows how warm the food has become, the note shows what was done, and the team knows where everything is.

b.label: Measure, move and log the deviation, but say nothing to the team.
b.explanation: The goods and the log are in order, but someone searches the wrong fridge in the middle of service.

c.label: Tell the team and move the goods over to the other fridge, but write nothing in the log.
c.explanation: The team knows where things stand, but nothing shows that the deviation was found and dealt with.

d.label: Write eight degrees in the log and turn the thermostat to its coldest setting.
d.explanation: An adjusted figure is worse than a deviation, and the goods stay in the warmth.

fail.outcome: The cheese and charcuterie are still in the warm fridge. Nobody has written anything.

halfGrip.analysis: The goods and the log were handled, but the team didn't know where everything was.
halfGrip.experience: The team knew where things stood, but the log says nothing.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: Sara opens the broken fridge in the middle of service.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: The log lies open on the same page as yesterday.

success.outcome: The goods are cold in the other fridge. The deviation is in the log with the time and the action.

staff.outcome: Nobody did anything about the fridge before opening.

staffTexts.success: The chef moves the goods and writes in the log.
staffTexts.fail: Nobody did anything about the fridge before opening.

vb07-provningen.title: A tasting for four
vb07-provningen.body: A party of four at table {bord} wants a tasting of three wines.

guestLine.a: One of the party says: “I'm driving home tonight, but I don't want to just sit and watch.”
guestLine.b: One of the party says: “I'm the driver tonight. Can I still join in?”

steps.question: In what order are three wines tasted?

a.label: Most expensive first, while the palate is fresh
a.explanation: The price says nothing about the order.

b.label: Fullest first, to warm up
b.explanation: A full wine takes over, and the light ones disappear afterwards.

c.label: Sweet first, to wake the appetite
c.explanation: Sweetness lingers and makes dry wines taste sour afterwards.

d.label: Light before full, dry before sweet
d.explanation: Each wine gets to show itself without the previous one taking over.

fail.outcome: The most powerful wine goes first. The guests think the rest taste thin.

steps.clue: Analysis: The order decides how the wines taste.

steps.question: What is the guest looking for?

a.label: As much as the others, they are small glasses
a.explanation: Three small glasses add up to a couple of glasses of wine, and the guest is driving.

b.label: To take part fully, without drinking
b.explanation: The guest wants to taste and compare. Tasting without drinking is possible.

c.label: Something of their own to drink meanwhile
c.explanation: Thoughtful, but a glass of their own still leaves them on the sidelines.

d.label: Not to take part
d.explanation: The guest said the opposite.

fail.outcome: The guest who is driving sits with full glasses and looks uncomfortable.

steps.clue: Experience: One guest is driving but wants to take part.

steps.question: How do you lay the table and pour?

a.label: A new tasting glass per wine, light before full, equal pours for all.
a.explanation: Glasses and order are right, but the guest who is driving cannot taste without drinking.

b.label: Whatever glasses are nearest, fullest first, the same for all.
b.explanation: Full first makes the rest thin, and the guest who is driving is left with full glasses.

fail.outcome: The table fills with glasses of every shape. So does the dish rack.

c.label: A new tasting glass per wine, light before full, spittoon and water on the table.
c.explanation: New glasses keep the aromas apart. Spitting is normal at a tasting, and the guest who drives can take full part. The bar takes its responsibility for serving alcohol.

d.label: Spittoon on the table, one glass each, rinsed with water between wines.
d.explanation: The guest can take part, but water dilutes the next wine. Rinse with a splash of the next wine instead, which is called seasoning the glass.

fail.outcome: The glasses are rinsed at the table. The next wine tastes thin.
fail.ongoing: The table compares wines that taste of water. The tasting goes quiet.

halfGrip.analysis: The tasting was well built, but the guest who drives could not take part.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: One guest sits with three full glasses in front of them.
halfGrip.experience: Everyone could take part, but water in the glass dilutes the next wine.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: The table compares wines that taste of water.

success.outcome: Twelve glasses in rows on the table. The guests compare and discuss, and one of them spits and laughs.

staff.outcome: The staff take whatever glasses are nearest.

staffTexts.success: Sara lays out tasting glasses and puts out a spittoon.
staffTexts.fail: The staff take whatever glasses are nearest.

vb08-sallskap-pa-fem.title: Five without a booking
vb08-sallskap-pa-fem.body: It is {klockan}. A party of five stand at the door without a booking.

guestLine.a: One of the party: “We've walked all day. We'll take anything, as long as we can sit together.”
guestLine.b: One of the party: “We're celebrating Lisa's doctorate! Do you have room for all of us?”

steps.question: What does a cover mean in restaurant language?

a.label: A table for two, laid for the evening
a.explanation: A table for two is called a two-top. A cover is a single place, so a two-top has two covers.

b.label: The bill left in a folder
b.explanation: The bill is often left in a folder, but that is not called a cover. Covers count guests, not money.

c.label: A guest's place with its table setting
c.explanation: A cover is a guest's place at the table with plate, cutlery and glasses. Five guests are five covers, and that is how the restaurant counts the evening.

d.label: A booking without a name
d.explanation: A booking without a name is not in the book. Cover is the word for a guest's place.

fail.outcome: {personal} counts tables instead of places and is unsure what is possible.

steps.clue: Analysis: Five guests are five covers.

steps.question: What is the party looking for?

a.label: A table straight away, anywhere
a.explanation: They want to sit soon, but they said "together".

b.label: A straight answer that it's full
b.explanation: They asked for a place, not for a no.

c.label: To sit together, soon, without having to move on
c.explanation: They are five who want to be five, and they want to stay here.

fail.outcome: The party leave. Two of them look in through the window.

steps.clue: Experience: The party wants to be together and to stay.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Check the table plan. Four at the four-top and the fifth at the bar.
a.explanation: Everyone gets a place without rearranging the room, but the party is split.

b.label: Push a four-top and a two-top together in the middle of the room, now, so all sit together.
b.explanation: Everyone sits together, but pushed-together tables in a full room take space, glasses and staff.

c.label: Say from the door that it's full tonight.
c.explanation: Saying no when there is room costs the evening's takings and gives a bad name.

d.label: Check the table plan, and let all five wait at the bar until the six-top is free.
d.explanation: The table plan shows what you can promise and when. All five stay together the whole time, and the room doesn't have to be rearranged.

fail.outcome: The party wait at the door while {personal} looks around the room.

halfGrip.analysis: Everyone got a place, but the fifth sat alone at the bar.
halfGrip.experience: The party sat together, but the room paid for it.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: One of the party keeps turning round towards the bar.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: The waiters squeeze past the pushed-together tables.

success.outcome: All five have a place. The party raises a toast, and the room flows on.

staff.outcome: The staff didn't know what they could promise. The party left.

staffTexts.success: Per checks the table plan and asks the party to have a glass at the bar.
staffTexts.fail: The staff didn't know what they could promise. The party left.

vb09-getosten.title: Wine with the goat's cheese
vb09-getosten.body: {gäst} at table {bord} orders the fresh goat's cheese with honey and asks which wine goes with it.

guestLine.a: “I only drink red. White wine feels like a weekday lunch to me.”
guestLine.b: “White isn't my thing. Have you got a red that works?”

steps.question: What marks the taste of a fresh goat's cheese?

a.label: A strong, aged, nutty taste
a.explanation: That applies to aged cheeses.

b.label: Sweetness, as in a cream cheese
b.explanation: The sweetness on the plate comes from the honey.

c.label: Fresh acidity and creaminess
c.explanation: The acidity is what the wine must meet, or the wine tastes flat.

d.label: Saltiness from brine
d.explanation: Brine belongs to cheeses like feta.

fail.outcome: You hesitate about the cheese, and the wine suggestion becomes a guess.

steps.clue: Analysis: The wine must stand up to the cheese's acidity.

steps.question: What is the guest looking for?

a.label: A red wine, and to have the wish taken seriously
a.explanation: The wish is not an obstacle. It says what to choose.

b.label: Something festive, the colour matters less
b.explanation: The guest said red and should be taken at their word.

c.label: To be convinced that a white wine suits the cheese best
c.explanation: The guest did not ask for a lesson.

fail.outcome: The guest gets a wine they did not want, or one that does not suit the cheese.

steps.clue: Experience: The guest wants red.

steps.question: What do you suggest?

a.label: The full, oaked Cabernet Sauvignon the guest is pointing at.
a.explanation: The guest gets their red, but strong tannins against tangy cheese give a bitter, metallic taste.

b.label: A dry Sancerre blanc, with a short word about the cheese.
b.explanation: A classic pairing, but the guest asked for red and feels overruled.

c.label: Say red does not go with goat's cheese and serve the house white.
c.explanation: That is not true, and the guest gets neither their wish nor a choice that suits the cheese.

fail.outcome: The guest tastes. The cheese and the wine pull in different directions.
fail.ongoing: The cheese stays on the plate. The guest drinks the wine on its own.

d.label: A light Sancerre rouge or Gamay, with soft tannins.
d.explanation: Low tannin and fresh acidity meet goat's cheese best among the reds. Sancerre rouge is made from Pinot Noir in the same area as Crottin de Chavignol.

fail.outcome: The guest tastes. The cheese and the wine pull in different directions.
fail.ongoing: The cheese stays on the plate. The guest drinks the wine on its own.

halfGrip.analysis: The wine met the cheese's acidity, but the guest asked for red and got white.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: The guest tastes politely and leaves half the glass.
halfGrip.experience: The guest got their red, but the tannins make the cheese bitter.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: The cheese stays on the plate. The guest drinks the wine on its own.

success.outcome: The guest tastes, nods and orders another glass.

staff.outcome: The guest gets the house red. It does not suit the cheese.

staffTexts.success: Per finds a Gamay and mentions that it suits the cheese.
staffTexts.fail: The guest gets the house red. It does not suit the cheese.

vb10-berusad.title: Another bottle
vb10-berusad.body: A guest at the bar has drunk a lot, is talking loudly and wants another bottle.

guestLine.a: The guest, loudly: “Come on, I'm a regular! One more bottle, I'm buying for the whole bar.”
guestLine.b: The guest, quietly: “I've had a rotten week. I just want one more bottle.”

steps.question: What does the Alcohol Act say about a visibly intoxicated guest?

a.label: A glass is fine, but not a bottle
a.explanation: Even a glass is serving a visibly intoxicated guest. The law makes no difference between a glass and a bottle.

fail.outcome: The guest gets a glass and calls for the next one.
fail.ongoing: The guest at the bar calls for the next glass.

b.label: No serving at all to a visibly intoxicated guest
b.explanation: The Alcohol Act forbids serving anyone who is visibly intoxicated. The alcohol licence is at stake, and that applies to every glass.

c.label: Regulars may be served at the staff's own judgement of the situation
c.explanation: Regular or not, the same law applies. Serving a visibly intoxicated guest can cost the alcohol licence.

fail.outcome: The bottle arrives. The voice at the bar gets louder.
fail.ongoing: The voice at the bar can be heard across the whole room. The guests nearby move away.

steps.clue: Analysis: No serving at all to a noticeably intoxicated guest.

steps.question: What is the guest looking for?

a.label: Not to lose face in front of the others, and that someone cares
a.explanation: A no can be accepted if it is given with respect. It is the humiliation that starts a fight.

b.label: To be taken seriously as a regular
b.explanation: That's true, but being a regular gives no right to be served.

c.label: To get the bottle
c.explanation: It is what the guest asks for, but not what they need.

fail.outcome: The guest stays at the bar and raises their voice.
fail.ongoing: The guest at the bar can be heard across the whole room.

steps.clue: Experience: The guest doesn't want to lose face.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Give one last glass, with water and bread, to keep things calm.
a.explanation: The care is right, but one last glass is still serving a noticeably intoxicated guest.

b.label: Serve the bottle, the guest is a regular and usually copes.
b.explanation: Regular or not, the same law applies, and the licence is at stake.

fail.outcome: The bottle arrives. The voice at the bar gets louder.
fail.ongoing: The voice at the bar can be heard across the whole room. The guests nearby move away.

c.label: Say no calmly and close to the guest, give water and food, and offer a taxi.
c.explanation: A quiet no keeps it private, water and food show care, and the taxi gets the guest home safely.

d.label: Say no clearly across the bar, and tell the guest to go home.
d.explanation: The no is right, but in front of an audience it becomes a fight about not losing face.

fail.outcome: The guest takes offence and starts arguing loudly.
fail.ongoing: The guest at the bar is arguing with the staff. The people nearby look over.

halfGrip.analysis: The no held, but the guest was humiliated in front of the bar.
halfGrip.experience: The guest calmed down, but the law was broken.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: The guest leaves and slams the door.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: The guest orders another glass ten minutes later.

success.outcome: The guest grumbles, but takes the water, a plate of bread and a taxi home.

staff.outcome: The staff keep serving the guest at the bar.

staffTexts.success: Elin calmly says no, puts out water and calls a taxi.
staffTexts.fail: The staff keep serving the guest at the bar.

vb11-cremant.title: Is it champagne?
vb11-cremant.body: {gäst} at table {bord} points at the sparkling wine by the glass and asks if it is champagne. It is a Crémant de Loire.

guestLine.a: “Crémant … sounds like champagne's little brother. I want to treat myself tonight.”
guestLine.b: “I got a new job today! Is crémant good enough for that?”

steps.question: What sets a crémant apart from champagne?

a.label: Nothing, it is more or less the same thing
a.explanation: Champagne is a protected designation of origin. Calling crémant champagne is misleading.

b.label: Only the price
b.explanation: Crémant is often cheaper, but it is the method and the origin that differ.

c.label: Crémant ferments in a tank, not in the bottle
c.explanation: Crémant is made by the traditional method, with the second fermentation in the bottle.

d.label: The same method, but made outside Champagne
d.explanation: The second fermentation happens in the bottle, as in champagne, but in other French regions.

fail.outcome: You answer that it is more or less champagne. Later the guest reads the label on the bottle.
fail.ongoing: The guest reads the label again and looks doubtful.

steps.clue: Analysis: It is not champagne, but made the same way.

steps.question: What is the guest looking for?

a.label: The cheapest sparkling there is
a.explanation: The guest wants a treat. It is about the feeling of a fine choice.

b.label: Champagne, just to be on the safe side for the evening
b.explanation: It might suit, but the guest asked about a glass.

c.label: A treat, and to know the choice is good
c.explanation: The guest hesitates over the word, not over the wine.

fail.outcome: The guest has a glass of red instead.

steps.clue: Experience: The guest wants to celebrate, but hesitates.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Say briefly that the method is the same, and offer a small taste.
a.explanation: The method sells a crémant, and a taste shows more than words. The guest chooses with the wine in their mouth.

b.label: Say that most people won't notice the difference anyway.
b.explanation: It sounds as if the guest doesn't understand. It sells neither the wine nor trust.

fail.outcome: The cork pops and wine foams over the tablecloth.

c.label: Suggest the champagne by the bottle instead, to make it festive.
c.explanation: Festive, but the guest asked about a glass, and the crémant was already a good choice.

d.label: Explain the method, the second fermentation and the designation of origin carefully.
d.explanation: All true, but the guest wanted to celebrate, not take a course.

fail.outcome: The cork pops and wine foams over the tablecloth.

halfGrip.analysis: The facts were right, but the guest wanted a treat. A taste would have said more.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: The guest nods politely and takes a glass of white.
halfGrip.experience: The evening became festive, but the crémant was already a good choice, made the same way.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: The guest gets a bottle of champagne and glances at the bill.

success.outcome: The guest tastes, smiles and orders a glass.

staff.outcome: The staff answer vaguely. The guest takes something else.

staffTexts.success: Sara lets the guest taste and says it is the same method.
staffTexts.fail: The staff answer vaguely. The guest takes something else.

vb12-varmt-rott.title: Too warm
vb12-varmt-rott.body: {gäst} at table {bord} sends back a glass of {vin}: it is too warm. The bottle has stood on the bar all evening.

guestLine.a: “It tastes like warm squash. I thought red was meant to be at room temperature, but this isn't nice.”
guestLine.b: “Sorry to complain, but is this really how it should be?”

steps.question: At what temperature does red wine taste best?

a.label: Room temperature, as in a warm bar
a.explanation: The rule comes from cool stone houses. A warm bar is too warm.

b.label: Cooler than the room: 14–16 for light, 16–18 for full
b.explanation: Then the alcohol is held back and the fruit is fresh.

c.label: Fridge cold, like a white
c.explanation: Red served too cold is tight and the tannins feel hard.

d.label: Temperature does not affect the taste
d.explanation: Red served too warm tastes of alcohol and jam.

fail.outcome: You agree that the wine is at the right temperature. The guest does not look convinced.

steps.clue: Analysis: The wine is warmer than it should be.

steps.question: What is the guest looking for?

a.label: An explanation of the old rule about room temperature for red wine
a.explanation: It is the wine that should be corrected, not the guest.

b.label: A different wine
b.explanation: Perhaps, but the guest chose this wine.

c.label: A cooler glass, and to hear they were right
c.explanation: The guest doubts themselves but tasted correctly.

fail.outcome: The guest takes the glass but does not smile.

steps.clue: Experience: The guest is unsure of their own judgement.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: A new glass from a cool bottle, and explain how heat affects wine.
a.explanation: The wine is right, but the guest got a lecture and never heard they were right.

b.label: Tell the guest they're right, thank them and add an ice cube.
b.explanation: The guest feels heard, but the ice dilutes the wine.

c.label: Agree, pour from a cool bottle, move open bottles to the fridge.
c.explanation: A cool wine fridge or a while in ice water saves it. The guest was right, and it should show.

d.label: Explain kindly that red wine is served at room temperature, as here.
d.explanation: In a warm bar the wine is too warm, and the guest is right.

fail.outcome: The guest drinks the glass without saying more.
fail.ongoing: The glass stands untouched. The guest at table {bord} orders nothing more.

halfGrip.analysis: The wine got cool, but the guest got a lecture instead of a thank you.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: The guest drinks in silence and orders nothing more.
halfGrip.experience: The guest was proved right, but the ice dilutes the wine. It is the bottle that should be chilled.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: The ice cube melts. The wine turns watery.

success.outcome: A new glass on the table. The guest tastes and nods. The open bottles are gone from the bar.

staff.outcome: The staff do not answer the complaint. The guest leaves the glass standing.

staffTexts.success: Per changes the glass and puts the bottles in the wine fridge.
staffTexts.fail: The staff do not answer the complaint. The guest leaves the glass standing.

vb13-delegationen.title: The delegation
vb13-delegationen.body: It is {klockan}. A delegation calls and wants to book the whole wine bar tomorrow, but wants the kitchen to do a test run of the new menu tonight so they can taste it.

guestLine.a: “We're twenty from the council. We want to be sure the food holds up.”
guestLine.b: “Our director has coeliac disease. We want to taste before we decide.”

steps.question: What is the purpose of a test run before a large booking?

a.label: To test dishes, portions and timings in advance
a.explanation: The test run shows how the menu tastes, how big the portions are and how long each dish takes. The guest gets to taste, and the kitchen finds out that it holds up.

b.label: To sell more food the same evening
b.explanation: The test run is a work task for the booking, not an extra sale. It costs time in the kitchen.

c.label: To let the guest choose which chef cooks
c.explanation: The guest tastes the menu, not the chefs. It is the dishes that are being tried.

fail.outcome: You promise a test run without knowing what it demands of the kitchen.

steps.clue: Analysis: A trial cook tests dishes, portions and timings.

steps.question: What is the delegation looking for?

a.label: Confidence: knowing that the evening will hold
a.explanation: They will answer for the evening in front of others. It is certainty they are buying.

b.label: To taste the new menu tonight, before they book
b.explanation: They asked for it, but a tasting tomorrow gives the same confidence.

c.label: The lowest price
c.explanation: They didn't mention the price, they mentioned the food.

fail.outcome: The delegation sounds doubtful. The booking hangs loose.

steps.clue: Experience: The delegation wants to be sure the evening will hold.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Take the booking and run the new menu tonight.
a.explanation: The delegation gets what it asked for, but changing the menu mid-service causes mistakes on the tickets.

b.label: Promise everything they ask for, and ask the kitchen afterwards.
b.explanation: A promise the kitchen can't keep becomes a let-down tomorrow.

c.label: Take the booking, confirm numbers and allergies, and do the trial cook tomorrow morning.
c.explanation: The booking is secure, the kitchen gets time to do the trial cook well, and the allergies are known from the start.

d.label: Take the booking and do the trial cook tomorrow morning, but without asking about allergies.
d.explanation: The plan holds, but the kitchen doesn't know what must be avoided, and the delegation notices.

fail.outcome: The menu is changed in the middle of service. Two orders have to be made again.
fail.ongoing: The kitchen changes menu in the middle of service. The orders sit still on the rail.

halfGrip.analysis: The booking was made, but the allergies were forgotten.
halfGrip.experience: The delegation got to taste, but tonight's guests paid the price.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: The phone rings again. The delegation is asking about the gluten.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: Two orders go back to the kitchen.

success.outcome: The booking is written down, the tasting has a time, and the evening goes on.

staff.outcome: The staff answer vaguely. The delegation books somewhere else.

staffTexts.success: Per takes the booking and asks the kitchen for a time tomorrow.
staffTexts.fail: The staff answer vaguely. The delegation books somewhere else.

vb14-surdegen.title: Sourdough and gluten
vb14-surdegen.body: {gäst} at table {bord} has coeliac disease and asks if the sourdough bread is fine. "Surely the fermentation removes the gluten?"

guestLine.a: The guest: “I got ill the last time I ate out. I just want to be able to eat bread like everyone else.”
guestLine.b: The guest, hopefully: “My doctor says no, but sourdough is supposed to be different?”

steps.question: What applies to sourdough bread with coeliac disease?

a.label: The fermentation removes the gluten, the bread is safe
a.explanation: That is a common myth. Sourdough bread made with wheat and rye contains gluten, and for someone with coeliac disease even small amounts damage the gut.

fail.outcome: The bread basket is put on the table.
fail.ongoing: The bread basket is on the table of the guest with coeliac disease.

b.label: A little bread is fine, as long as the amount is small
b.explanation: With coeliac disease there is no harmless small amount. It is not a question of how much, but of whether there is gluten at all.

c.label: Rye sourdough is safe, only wheat has gluten
c.explanation: Rye also contains gluten, as does barley. Rye bread is not safe with coeliac disease.

d.label: Sourdough made with wheat, rye or barley has gluten
d.explanation: Sourdough fermentation breaks down some of the gluten, but far from enough. For someone with coeliac disease, sourdough bread made with wheat, rye or barley is not safe.

fail.outcome: The guest takes a slice, hesitantly.
fail.ongoing: The guest with coeliac disease eats a slice of bread.

steps.clue: Analysis: Sourdough made from wheat, rye or barley contains gluten.

steps.question: What is the guest looking for?

a.label: Something safe with the cheese, without any fuss
a.explanation: The guest wants to eat like the others at the table, and not have to worry.

b.label: A careful explanation of how gluten and fermentation work in bread
b.explanation: It may be interesting, but the guest wants to eat.

c.label: To hear that the sourdough is fine
c.explanation: The guest hopes so, but a yes would be dangerous.

fail.outcome: The next dish leaves the kitchen without anyone knowing about the coeliac disease.

steps.clue: Experience: The guest wants to eat like everyone else, but safely.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Gluten-free bread on a clean board in its own basket, but the kitchen isn't told.
a.explanation: The bread is safe, but gluten can be in sauces, fried food and croutons in the next dish.

b.label: Say the kitchen will make something nice, and put the gluten-free bread in the usual basket.
b.explanation: The guest feels looked after, but the sourdough crumbs are still in the basket.

c.label: Say the sourdough is fine, the fermentation removes most of it.
c.explanation: It is a common myth. For someone with coeliac disease even small amounts do harm.

fail.outcome: The bread basket is put on the table.
fail.ongoing: The bread basket is on the table of the guest with coeliac disease.

d.label: Gluten-free bread on a clean board, in its own basket, and tell the kitchen at once.
d.explanation: Clean utensils and a separate basket keep the crumbs away, and the kitchen knows before the next dish is cooked.

fail.outcome: The gluten-free bread has been lying among sourdough crumbs.

success.outcome: The guest gets gluten-free crackers with the cheese and says thank you.

staff.outcome: The staff answer that it will probably be fine.

staffTexts.success: Sara brings out gluten-free bread on a clean board and goes to the kitchen.
staffTexts.fail: The staff answer that it will probably be fine.

vb15-fisken.title: The fish
vb15-fisken.body: The supplier calls: the Arctic char for tonight's tartare arrived with a broken cold chain. It is probably fine, but it cannot be traced. New fish arrives on Thursday.

guestLine.a: The guest: “We've driven here for your char tartare, everyone talks about it.”
guestLine.b: The guest: “The tartare, please. My wife has talked about it all week.”

steps.question: What does a broken cold chain mean for raw fish?

a.label: The fish has been too warm for an unknown time
a.explanation: Nobody knows how long or how warm the fish has been. Bacteria may have grown without it showing or smelling.

b.label: That the fish is spoiled and smells bad
b.explanation: It may be spoiled, but that does not have to show or smell. The uncertainty is the problem.

c.label: Nothing, as long as the fish smells fresh
c.explanation: The nose does not reveal bacteria that can make guests ill. Raw fish needs an unbroken cold chain.

fail.outcome: You take the call from the supplier lightly.

steps.clue: Analysis: Nobody knows how long the fish was too warm.

steps.question: What are the guests looking for?

a.label: The tartare, whatever it costs
a.explanation: They want a good evening, not a risk.

b.label: An evening that lives up to what they have heard
b.explanation: It is the experience they came for. The tartare was the way there.

c.label: To know exactly what happened with the delivery of the fish
c.explanation: Honest, but the details may make them worried about the rest of the food.

fail.outcome: The guests look disappointed and order less.

steps.clue: Experience: The guests came for something special.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Take the tartare off, and just say it has run out for tonight.
a.explanation: The guest is disappointed without getting anything instead.

b.label: Serve the tartare as usual, after all the guests have driven all the way here just for that dish.
b.explanation: Raw fish with a broken cold chain and no traceability is a risk the restaurant takes on the guest's behalf.

c.label: Say the chef is ill tonight.
c.explanation: A lie is unnecessary, and here the truth works in the restaurant's favour.

d.label: Take the tartare off, say honestly that the fish wasn't good enough, and suggest the beetroot.
d.explanation: A short, honest answer shows that the kitchen cares about quality, and a suggestion gives the disappointment a new dish to try.

fail.outcome: The tartare goes out. Nobody asks about the fish.
fail.ongoing: The tartare goes out plate by plate. In the kitchen they look at each other.

success.outcome: The board is rewritten. Roast beetroot with chèvre takes the tartare's place, and the guests order it.

staff.outcome: The kitchen uses the fish without asking.

staffTexts.success: The chef takes the tartare off and puts the beetroot forward.
staffTexts.fail: The kitchen uses the fish without asking.

vb16-stamgasten.title: The regular's table
vb16-stamgasten.body: A regular comes in and wants their usual window table, table {bord}. It is booked for a couple arriving in a quarter of an hour.

guestLine.a: The regular: “Hi! My usual table, right? I've been looking forward to it all week.”
guestLine.b: The regular: “I've brought my sister tonight. I've told her about the window table.”

steps.question: Who has the right to a booked table?

a.label: The regular, who always sits there
a.explanation: A habit gives no right to a table. The booking is a promise to someone else.

b.label: Whoever booked it, from the booked time
b.explanation: A booking is a promise. The couple who booked should get the table they were promised.

c.label: Whoever gets to the table first
c.explanation: Then the booking would be worthless. Whoever booked has already taken their place in advance.

fail.outcome: You hesitate at the door, and the regular notices.

steps.clue: Analysis: The booking is a promise to someone else.

steps.question: What is the regular looking for?

a.label: To go ahead of other guests who have booked
a.explanation: The regular asked for their table, not to jump the queue.

b.label: To be recognised and to feel at home
b.explanation: It is not the table itself, but being someone here.

c.label: The window table, whatever it takes
c.explanation: It is what the regular asks for, but what they want is to be seen.

fail.outcome: The regular leaves.
fail.ongoing: The regular's usual place by the window stands empty.

steps.clue: Experience: The regular wants to be seen.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Greet them politely, say the table is booked and show them another.
a.explanation: The booking holds, but the regular is treated like anyone else.

b.label: Greet them by name and give the regular the window table. The couple will have to move.
b.explanation: The regular is happy, but the couple who booked don't get what they were promised.

c.label: Check the list first, and then say the table is taken.
c.explanation: The regular stands waiting, and then gets a short no.

d.label: Greet them by name, explain that it's booked, and offer a glass.
d.explanation: The name shows they are recognised, honesty keeps the promise to the couple, and the glass makes the no warm.

fail.outcome: The regular stands at the door for a while before anyone comes over.

halfGrip.analysis: The booking held, but the regular felt like anyone else.
halfGrip.experience: The regular got their table, but the couple didn't get theirs.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: The regular drinks their glass and leaves early.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: The couple who booked look around for the window table.

success.outcome: The regular sits down at the bar with a glass and smiles.

staff.outcome: The staff say the table is taken. The regular leaves.

staffTexts.success: Per greets them by name and offers a glass at the bar.
staffTexts.fail: The staff say the table is taken. The regular leaves.

vb17-glasen.title: Out of glasses
vb17-glasen.body: It is {klockan}. Five orders are waiting at the bar, and {personal} says the wine glasses have run out. The dishwasher has twenty minutes left.

guestLine.a: A guest at the bar: “We ordered ten minutes ago. Have you forgotten us?”
guestLine.b: Sara: “Five orders are waiting, and the tables are looking this way.”

steps.question: Why does a wine glass have a rounded bowl that narrows towards the top?

a.label: So the wine stays cold for longer in the glass through the evening
a.explanation: It is the foot and the stem that protect the wine from the warmth of your hand. The shape of the bowl is about the aroma.

b.label: So the glass copes better with the dishwasher
b.explanation: The shape has nothing to do with washing. Thin wine glasses are, if anything, fragile in the machine.

c.label: The bowl gathers the aroma and guides it towards the nose
c.explanation: The wine can be swirled in the bowl, and the narrower opening holds the aroma in. That is why the same wine tastes of more in a wine glass than in a water glass.

fail.outcome: The orders stand still while the staff look for glasses.

steps.clue: Analysis: The bowl gathers the aroma. It is the wine glass that makes the wine.

steps.question: What do those who are waiting need?

a.label: To know why the glasses have run out
a.explanation: An explanation helps a little, but what they need is to know when.

b.label: An answer, and for the wait to be fair
b.explanation: Guests put up with a wait they know about and that goes in turn.

c.label: The wine straight away, in any glass at the bar
c.explanation: They ordered wine at a wine bar. Wine in a water glass says the bar can't cope with its evening.

fail.outcome: Two tables wait and watch others get their wine first.

steps.clue: Experience: Those who are waiting want to know they haven't been forgotten.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Hand-wash and polish glasses, and serve in turn without saying anything.
a.explanation: The glasses and the order are right, but anyone waiting without a word thinks they've been forgotten.

b.label: Tell everyone there will be a wait, and pour the wine into water glasses for now.
b.explanation: The word is right, but wine in water glasses costs the aroma and the reputation.

c.label: Give the first glasses to those who ordered a whole bottle.
c.explanation: Those who ordered a glass wait longest, and they remember being skipped.

d.label: Hand-wash and polish glasses, tell those who are waiting, and serve in turn.
d.explanation: Empty glasses on the tables are the evening's stock, and a short word makes the wait understandable.

fail.outcome: The wine arrives in water glasses. Someone at table {bord} takes a photo of it.
fail.ongoing: Wine in water glasses goes out to the tables. The guests hold them up to the light.

halfGrip.analysis: The glasses were right, but nobody was told anything.
halfGrip.experience: Everyone knew what was happening, but the wine came in water glasses.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: A table keeps waving for the staff.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: Someone at the table photographs the glass.

success.outcome: Polished glasses go out in the right order, and the queue at the bar moves again.

staff.outcome: The wine is served in whatever glasses there are.

staffTexts.success: Sara hand-washes glasses and tells the tables.
staffTexts.fail: The wine is served in whatever glasses there are.

vb18-kavajen.title: Wine on the jacket
vb18-kavajen.body: {personal} drops a bottle of {vin} at table {bord}. It breaks, and wine splashes onto a guest's pale jacket.

guestLine.a: The guest looks down at the jacket and says quietly: “It was my father's. I only wear it when there's something special.”
guestLine.b: The guest looks down at the jacket: “I bought it for my thesis defence. It's the first time I've worn it since.”

steps.question: What in red wine stains the fabric?

a.label: Pigments from the grape skins, anthocyanins
a.explanation: Red wine's colour comes from the skins, and those pigments are what stick in the fabric.

b.label: The tannins from the oak barrel
b.explanation: Tannins give grip, but the colour comes from the skins.

c.label: The alcohol, which burns in the colour
c.explanation: Alcohol does not stain.

fail.outcome: The staff stand uncertainly beside the guest while the stain spreads.

steps.clue: Analysis: The stain is fresh, and the colour sets easily.

steps.question: What is the guest looking for?

a.label: Compensation for the jacket
a.explanation: Dry cleaning is part of it, but the guest talked about what the jacket means.

b.label: That the jacket is taken seriously and someone looks after them
b.explanation: The jacket is not just any garment.

c.label: For it to be quick and no fuss made
c.explanation: Brushing an accident aside turns it into an insult.

fail.outcome: The glass is swept up. The guest stays seated with a red stain.
fail.ongoing: The guest with the stained jacket stays seated, looking at the stain.

steps.clue: Experience: The jacket means a lot to the guest.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Apologise and rub the stain out straight away with some warm water.
a.explanation: The care is right, but rubbing and heat press the colour in and set it.

b.label: Apologise, cold water to dab with, and pay the dry cleaning.
b.explanation: Cold water and dabbing lift the wine without setting the colour. The guest decides about their own jacket.
b.success: The guest dabs the stain and says thank you.

c.label: Apologise, cold water, dry cleaning and tonight's wine on the house.
c.explanation: The same correct handling, and a gesture that turns the accident into a story of how the bar looked after its guest. It costs more, but the reputation grows more.
c.success: The guest laughs a little and raises a glass with the party. The next table has seen it all.

d.label: Give cold water to dab with, sweep up and move on.
d.explanation: The stain is handled right, but without an apology the accident becomes an insult.

fail.outcome: The stain gets bigger and darker. The guest sighs.

halfGrip.analysis: The stain was handled right, but the jacket meant something and nobody apologised.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: The guest dabs alone with a napkin and pays early.
halfGrip.experience: The care was right, but warm water and rubbing set the colour in the fabric.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: The stain grows larger and darker.

success.outcome: The guest dabs the stain and says thank you.

staff.outcome: The glass is swept up, and someone apologises briefly.

staffTexts.success: Mira fetches cold water and apologises.
staffTexts.fail: The glass is swept up, and someone apologises briefly.

vb19-bongarna.title: The tickets pile up
vb19-bongarna.body: It is {klockan} and the kitchen is behind. Twelve order tickets hang on the rail, and {personal} says the small plates will take twenty minutes.

guestLine.a: The guest at the table that has waited longest: “Excuse me, have you forgotten us?”
guestLine.b: The chef: “They just keep coming. I can't keep up.”

steps.question: What does first in, first out mean on the ticket rail?

a.label: The simplest dishes are cooked first
a.explanation: Then those who ordered something complicated wait longest. First in, first out is about when the ticket came in.

b.label: The ticket that came in first is cooked first
b.explanation: The tickets are taken in the order they came in. That makes the wait fair, and nobody is forgotten.

c.label: The table closest to the kitchen gets its food first
c.explanation: Where the table is makes no difference. It is the time on the ticket that counts.

fail.outcome: The kitchen does not know which ticket to take first. The plates sit waiting.

steps.clue: Analysis: The ticket that came first is cooked first.

steps.question: What do the waiting tables need?

a.label: An honest answer about the time, and something to keep them going
a.explanation: A wait is easier to bear when you know how long it is.

b.label: For the food to come as fast as it possibly can, in any order at all
b.explanation: Then those who have waited longest wait even longer.

c.label: For someone to calm them down
c.explanation: It helps, but a calming word without an answer doesn't last long.

fail.outcome: The table waves more and more urgently. The guests look at the clock.

steps.clue: Experience: Those who have waited longest need an answer first.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Let the kitchen take the tickets in order, and wait to say anything until the food is ready.
a.explanation: The kitchen works correctly, but the silence makes the wait feel longer.

b.label: Go to the tables and promise the food will come in five minutes.
b.explanation: The guests calm down for a while, but a promise that isn't kept makes them angrier than the wait.

c.label: Ask the kitchen to do the simplest dishes first, no matter which ticket came in first on the rail.
c.explanation: The order breaks, the kitchen gets confused, and the right food ends up at the wrong table.

d.label: Tell the tables the honest time, offer bread, and let the kitchen take the tickets in order.
d.explanation: An answer and bread buy time, and the order makes the wait fair.

fail.outcome: The kitchen jumps between tickets. Two tables get the wrong dish.
fail.ongoing: Wrong dishes go out and come back. The kitchen jumps between tickets.

halfGrip.analysis: The kitchen worked in order, but the tables got no answer.
halfGrip.experience: The tables calmed down, but the promise didn't hold.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: A table looks at the clock and whispers.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: Five minutes later no food has come. The guest raises a hand again.

success.outcome: The tables know how long they are waiting, the bread goes out, and the kitchen calmly works its way through the rail.

staff.outcome: Nobody says anything to the tables, and the kitchen takes the tickets as it gets to them.

staffTexts.success: Per goes from table to table with an answer and bread.
staffTexts.fail: Nobody says anything to the tables, and the kitchen takes the tickets as it gets to them.

vb20-notan.title: A wrong bill
vb20-notan.body: {gäst} at table {bord} has been given a bill with two bottles too many. The guest is upset and speaking loudly.

guestLine.a: The guest, loudly: “Two bottles we never ordered! Are you trying to cheat us?”
guestLine.b: The guest, tight-lipped: “This is the second time I've had a wrong bill here.”

steps.question: What lets the guest check their bill?

a.label: The total being at the top
a.explanation: The total does not say what it is made up of. The guest cannot see what has gone wrong.

b.label: The VAT being printed
b.explanation: The VAT must be shown, but it does not show what the guest has ordered.

c.label: The table number being on the bill
c.explanation: The table number shows which table the bill is for, not what is on it.

d.label: Every dish and bottle being listed with quantity and price
d.explanation: An itemised bill lets the guest see line by line what was ordered. Then two bottles too many show up straight away.

fail.outcome: The guest waves the bill and demands to know what it is made up of.

steps.clue: Analysis: An itemised bill shows the mistake line by line.

steps.question: What is the guest looking for?

a.label: An explanation of how the till works
a.explanation: An explanation sounds like a defence.

b.label: To be believed, and for it to be corrected at once
b.explanation: The guest doesn't want to leave feeling cheated.

c.label: To have the whole bill written off
c.explanation: It calms things down, but it is more than the mistake, and the guest didn't ask for it.

fail.outcome: The guest pays nothing and leaves, and the party goes with them.
fail.ongoing: There is whispering at the tables about the wrong bill.

steps.clue: Experience: The guest wants to be believed.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Go through the lines, correct the till and print a new bill.
a.explanation: The bill is right, but without an apology the guest is left with their anger.

b.label: Apologise at once, and write off the whole bill without going through the lines with the guest.
b.explanation: The guest calms down, but the mistake is never found, and the till doesn't add up.

c.label: Say the bill matches the till and can't be changed.
c.explanation: The till can be wrong. A guest who isn't listened to goes and tells people about it.

d.label: Go through the lines with the guest, apologise, correct the till and offer coffee.
d.explanation: The guest sees the mistake found and corrected, and the till matches the payment.

fail.outcome: The guest is left with a bill that still does not add up.

halfGrip.analysis: The bill was corrected, but the guest got no apology.
halfGrip.experience: The guest calmed down, but nobody knows where the mistake was.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: The guest pays without looking up.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: The same mistake shows up on the next bill.

success.outcome: The bill is corrected. The guest calms down and takes the coffee.

staff.outcome: The guest has to wait for the manager, who never comes.

staffTexts.success: Per goes through the bill with the guest and corrects it in the till.
staffTexts.fail: The guest has to wait for the manager, who never comes.

vb21-skuren-hand.title: A cut hand
vb21-skuren-hand.body: {personal} cuts their hand while opening a bottle with a knife. The blood soaks through the napkin.

guestLine.a: {personal}: “It's nothing, I'll grit my teeth. You can't manage without me tonight.”
guestLine.b: {personal}, pale: “Sorry. I'll just put a plaster on and carry on.”

steps.question: Which bacterium from wounds and skin can cause food poisoning?

a.label: Salmonella
a.explanation: Salmonella usually comes from poultry, eggs and contaminated food, not from a wound on the hand.

b.label: Listeria
b.explanation: Listeria is found in chilled foods such as cured fish and soft cheeses. It does not spread from wounds.

c.label: Staphylococcus aureus
c.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus thrives in wounds and on skin. It can produce toxins in food, which is why wounds must always be covered.

fail.outcome: Nobody understands why the wound matters. {personal} wipes their hand on the apron.

steps.clue: Analysis: Wounds near food must be covered. Staphylococci thrive in wounds.

steps.question: What does {personal} need?

a.label: To be looked after, and to stay in the team
a.explanation: They don't want to let the team down. It is possible to take care of both the wound and the will.

b.label: To carry on exactly as usual
b.explanation: The will is good, but an injured hand near open food is a risk to them and to the guests.

c.label: To be sent home at once
c.explanation: It may be right with a deep cut, but they want to stay and can.

fail.outcome: The team does not know who does what. Two people do the same thing.

steps.clue: Experience: {personal} doesn't want to let the team down.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Let them rest in the staff room and take their place yourself, without sanitising the surface.
a.explanation: The care is right, but the surface where the wound bled is used again.

b.label: Put on a plaster and let them carry on at their station, since they want to.
b.explanation: A plaster without a glove near open food is not enough.

c.label: Plaster and glove, sanitise the surface, move them to the till and tell the team.
c.explanation: The wound is covered, the surface is clean, and everyone knows who does what.

d.label: Plaster and glove, sanitise the surface, and send them home at once.
d.explanation: The hygiene is right, but the team gets thin, and they feel sent away.

fail.outcome: {personal} carries on. The plaster comes off by the sink.
fail.ongoing: The plaster keeps coming off. The chef is working with one hand.

halfGrip.analysis: The wound and the surface were handled, but the team lost a person.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: Two people run between the same stations.

success.outcome: The hand is dressed, the surface sanitised, and {personal} takes the till for the rest of the evening.

staff.outcome: Nobody sees to the wound, and {personal} keeps working.

staffTexts.success: Per dresses the hand, sanitises the counter and takes over the station.
staffTexts.fail: Nobody sees to the wound, and {personal} keeps working.

vb22-recensenten.title: Someone taking notes
vb22-recensenten.body: {gäst} at table {bord} is taking notes in a small book, photographing every dish and asking where the wines come from. {personal} whispers that it might be a critic.

guestLine.a: The guest: “Who made this wine, and why is it on your list?”
guestLine.b: {personal}, whispering: “It must be a critic. Should we give them something extra?”

steps.question: What does a designation of origin such as AOC or DOCG on a wine label indicate?

a.label: A defined area with its own rules for the wine
a.explanation: The designation of origin shows that the wine comes from a specific area and follows its rules, for example on grapes and growing.

b.label: That the wine is organically grown and certified by an inspector
b.explanation: Organic growing has its own labels. The designation of origin is about place and rules.

c.label: That the wine has won a medal
c.explanation: Medals are awarded at competitions. The designation of origin is not an award.

fail.outcome: The guest writes something down and looks up with raised eyebrows.

steps.clue: Analysis: The appellation names an area with its own rules.

steps.question: What is the guest looking for?

a.label: To be left in peace with their notes for the whole of the dinner
a.explanation: Partly, but the guest is asking questions and wants answers.

b.label: Knowledgeable answers, and the same evening as everyone else
b.explanation: A critic wants to see how the restaurant is, not how it can be for one evening.

c.label: Extra attention and tasters
c.explanation: Critics notice when they are treated differently, and the neighbouring tables notice too.

fail.outcome: The table gets tasters. The neighbouring tables notice.
fail.ongoing: The neighbouring tables watch the tasters go past them to the same table.

steps.clue: Experience: The guest wants to see the restaurant as it is.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Answer all of their questions about the wine carefully, and send a few extra tasters over to the table.
a.explanation: The answers are good, but the special treatment shows, to the neighbouring tables too.

b.label: Give the same service as to everyone, and read out what is on the label.
b.explanation: The right attitude, but the guest can read. A good answer explains what the label means.

c.label: Guess rather than say you don't know, it sounds more knowledgeable.
c.explanation: A wrong guess shows at once to someone who knows.

d.label: Show the bottle, talk about the area and the producer, and give the same service as to everyone.
d.explanation: A knowledgeable answer makes the origin concrete, and the service holds for every table.

fail.outcome: The answer does not match the label. The guest writes at length.

halfGrip.analysis: The answers were knowledgeable, but the table was treated differently.
halfGrip.experience: The service was even, but the answer was thin.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: The neighbouring table looks at the tasters and then at their own glasses.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: The guest writes something short and closes the notebook.

success.outcome: The guest takes notes and smiles at the answer about the wine.

staff.outcome: Everyone gets nervous, and the table is forgotten for a long while.

staffTexts.success: Elin shows the bottle and talks about the producer.
staffTexts.fail: Everyone gets nervous, and the table is forgotten for a long while.

vb23-sott.title: Something sweet
vb23-sott.body: Table {bord} wants to finish with the chocolate truffle and asks what to drink with it.

guestLine.a: The host says: “We want to finish with something that feels like a present.” One of the party puts a hand over their glass.
guestLine.b: The host says: “Something nice to toast with at the end!” One of the party says quietly that they don't drink alcohol.

steps.question: What happens to a dry wine with a sweet dessert?

a.label: It tastes sweeter
a.explanation: The opposite. Sweetness in the food makes the wine taste less sweet.

b.label: It tastes fuller
b.explanation: The wine loses fruit and feels thinner.

c.label: Nothing, sweetness only affects the food
c.explanation: Sweetness in food always affects how the wine tastes.

d.label: It tastes sourer and thinner
d.explanation: That is why the wine should be at least as sweet as the dessert.

fail.outcome: The guests get a suggestion that does not fit and look doubtful.

steps.clue: Analysis: The dessert is sweet, and that affects the wine.

steps.question: What is the table looking for?

a.label: Something festive for those who drink wine, nothing for the other
a.explanation: That is part of it, but one at the table needs something too.

b.label: To round off quickly, with coffee and the bill
b.explanation: The host asked for an ending to remember.

c.label: An ending for the whole table, including the one who doesn't drink
c.explanation: Everyone should be able to raise a glass.

fail.outcome: One guest sits without a glass while the others raise a toast.

steps.clue: Experience: One at the table doesn't drink.

steps.question: What do you serve with the truffle?

a.label: A glass of dry red for everyone, since red always goes with chocolate.
a.explanation: The sweetness makes the wine sour, and the guest who doesn't drink gets a glass they don't want.

b.label: A little ruby port; ask the non-drinker what they'd like.
b.explanation: A young, fruity port stands up to the chocolate's sweetness and bitterness. Sweet reds like Banyuls or Maury work too. A suggestion of their own for the guest who doesn't drink shows that their choice counts.

c.label: Dry sparkling for everyone, and alcohol-free bubbles for the one who doesn't drink.
c.explanation: Everyone raises a glass, but a dry wine turns sour against the chocolate.

d.label: Ruby port for everyone, and the one who doesn't drink can leave it.
d.explanation: The wine is right, but a glass the guest doesn't want singles them out.

fail.outcome: The guests taste. The wine turns sour and thin against the chocolate.
fail.ongoing: The sparkling wine sits untouched in the glasses next to the truffle.

halfGrip.analysis: The port carried the chocolate, but the guest who doesn't drink got a glass they didn't want.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: An untouched glass of port stands in front of one guest.
halfGrip.experience: Everyone could toast, but a dry wine turns sour against a sweet dessert.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: The guests taste and grimace a little at the chocolate.

success.outcome: The whole table raises a glass to the truffle.

staff.outcome: The table gets the evening's red with the chocolate.

staffTexts.success: Sara pours port and asks the one who doesn't drink what they would like.
staffTexts.fail: The table gets the evening's red with the chocolate.

vb24-terroir.title: What is terroir?
vb24-terroir.body: Things calm down. {gäst} at the bar asks {personal} what the word terroir on the wine list actually means. Two new guests are just coming in.

guestLine.a: The guest: “I've read the word a hundred times, but never understood it.”
guestLine.b: The guest: “My daughter is training to be a sommelier. I want to be able to keep up.”

steps.question: What does terroir mean?

a.label: The soil where the grapes grow
a.explanation: The soil is part of it, but terroir also covers climate, site and craft.

b.label: The combined influence of the place: soil, climate, site and people's craft
b.explanation: Terroir is the combined influence of the place on the wine: soil, climate, site and local tradition. The word is also used in the world of food, for example about cheese.

c.label: A French word for organic
c.explanation: Terroir has nothing to do with organic growing. It is about the influence of the place on the wine.

fail.outcome: The guest looks doubtful.
fail.ongoing: The guest at the bar loses interest in the wine list.

steps.clue: Analysis: Terroir is the combined influence of the place.

steps.question: What is the guest looking for?

a.label: To understand, with the wine in the glass
a.explanation: The guest wants to grasp it, not just hear a definition.

b.label: A long explanation
