b.explanation: Words help, but it is the comparison in the glass that shows the place.

c.label: To be recommended the most expensive wine on the list
c.explanation: The price says nothing about the place.

fail.outcome: Someone at the bar is left standing without being noticed.

steps.clue: Experience: The guest wants to understand, and two new guests are waiting.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Pour the same grape from two places side by side, and welcome the new ones meanwhile.
a.explanation: The same grape means the difference comes from the place, and the guest has something to do while you greet the new ones.

b.label: Pour the same grape from two places, and stay to finish the conversation.
b.explanation: The comparison is right, but the new guests are left standing without being seen.

c.label: Say you'll be right back, welcome the new ones, and then describe the aroma in words to the guest.
c.explanation: Nobody is left standing, but the guest gets nothing to taste.

d.label: Pour a glass of the most expensive wine, it says it all.
d.explanation: With nothing to compare it with, you can't taste what the place does.

fail.outcome: The guest tastes but finds nothing to hold on to.

halfGrip.analysis: The guest understood, but the new ones stood waiting.
halfGrip.experience: Everyone was seen, but terroir stayed just words.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: The two new guests go out again.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: The guest nods politely but orders nothing.

success.outcome: The guest compares the glasses, nods and orders one of the wines.

staff.outcome: The guest is told it's hard to explain.

staffTexts.success: Elin pours two glasses and welcomes the new guests.
staffTexts.fail: The guest is told it's hard to explain.

vb25-efter-stangning.title: After closing
vb25-efter-stangning.body: It is nearly eleven and the kitchen has closed. A party of three knocks and wants one last bottle. The staff have started cleaning.

guestLine.a: One of the party: “Please, just one glass. Our friend turns fifty today.”
guestLine.b: Per, tired: “We've cleaned half the bar. Don't tell me we're opening again.”

steps.question: What decides how late the wine bar may serve alcohol?

a.label: How long the kitchen is open
a.explanation: The kitchen can close before the bar. It is the serving hours in the licence that set the limit for alcohol.

b.label: When the staff go home according to the rota
b.explanation: The rota says who is working, not what you are allowed to do. The limit is in the alcohol licence.

c.label: The serving hours in the alcohol licence
c.explanation: The licence states when serving must stop. If that time has not passed you may serve, and then the question is not whether you may but whether you should.

fail.outcome: Nobody knows for sure what applies. The party stands in the doorway while the staff discuss it.

steps.clue: Analysis: The licence sets the limit, not the kitchen.

steps.question: What does the evening need?

a.label: A kind gesture to the guests, and a closing that works for the team
a.explanation: Both are right: the guests want to end well, and the team wants to go home.

b.label: That the party gets a whole bottle and can sit on as long as they like
b.explanation: Energy used up tonight is missing tomorrow.

c.label: A no, it's closed
c.explanation: Right by the opening hours, but it gives a colder name than it needs to.

fail.outcome: The bottle is opened. The staff stay another hour.

steps.clue: Experience: Both the guests and the team need something.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: A glass each, in glasses from the dish rack that look clean.
a.explanation: The gesture is right, but a glass that looks clean can still have grease and detergent on it.

b.label: Let them into the dining room and ask the chef to put together a cheese board for them.
b.explanation: The kitchen has already been cleaned. Starting it again costs more energy than it gives.

c.label: A glass each from an opened bottle, in clean glasses at the end of the bar.
c.explanation: An opened bottle has to be sold soon anyway, and the cleaning can carry on around the guests.

d.label: Say kindly that you've closed for the evening, and wish them a good night.
d.explanation: The team gets to go home, but a place that turns guests away at the door loses warmth.

fail.outcome: The glasses are smeared and the wine tastes flat. The party exchange disappointed looks.

halfGrip.analysis: The team got home on time, but the party left disappointed.
halfGrip.experience: The guests got their glass, but the glasses were smeared.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: The party walks on down the street, and nobody looks back.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: A guest wipes the rim of the glass with a napkin.

success.outcome: Three glasses at the bar. The party says thank you and leaves after half an hour, and the bar is done on time.

staff.outcome: The party is allowed to stay a long time, and the closing drags on.

staffTexts.success: Per pours three glasses at the end of the bar and carries on cleaning.
staffTexts.fail: The party is allowed to stay a long time, and the closing drags on.

vb26-oppna-flaskor.title: Open bottles
vb26-oppna-flaskor.body: The evening is over. Nine opened bottles are left, white and red, some of them half full.

guestLine.a: Elin, with her jacket on: “Shall we just pour them away? I want to go home.”
guestLine.b: Per: “Yesterday a tired glass went out. The guest put it down after one sip.”

steps.question: What is it that mainly spoils the wine in an opened bottle?

a.label: The light in the bar
a.explanation: Strong light can harm wine over time, but in an opened bottle it is the air that does the most damage overnight.

b.label: The cork drying out
b.explanation: A dry cork is a problem for bottles stored for a long time. An opened bottle is spoiled by the air that has got in.

c.label: The bottle standing upright
c.explanation: Upright is good for an opened bottle: less surface in contact with the air. The oxygen is the problem.

d.label: Oxygen oxidising the wine
d.explanation: Once the bottle is open, oxygen gets in and the wine loses fruit and freshness day by day. Cold slows this down, for red wine too.

fail.outcome: The staff do not know what needs protecting. The bottles are left standing while everyone waits for a decision.

steps.clue: Analysis: Oxygen spoils the wine. Cold slows it down.

steps.question: What do tonight and tomorrow need?

a.label: That everything is poured away now so that everyone gets home on time
a.explanation: It pours away money that could be saved.

b.label: That every bottle is tasted carefully now
b.explanation: It can be done tomorrow, when it is needed.

c.label: That the wine is saved, without the team staying late
c.explanation: Doing it right takes five minutes, and it saves the evening's margin.

fail.outcome: A glass that tastes tired goes out. The guest puts it down after one sip.

steps.clue: Experience: The team wants to go home, and tomorrow the wine should taste good.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Vacuum-seal, store cool, write the date, and taste before selling by the glass tomorrow.
a.explanation: Vacuum, cold and a date keep the wine for a couple of days, and tasting decides what can be sold.

b.label: Vacuum-seal, store cool and write the date, and then sell by the glass without tasting first.
b.explanation: The storage is right, but a wine may have lost more than expected. The guest notices before you do.

c.label: Put the corks back in on the counter, and let everyone go home at once.
c.explanation: The team gets home, but warmth and oxygen take the fruit out of the wine by tomorrow.

d.label: Pour away whatever is left, opened bottles don't keep anyway.
d.explanation: A half-full wine often keeps for a couple of days if it is stored correctly.

fail.outcome: Nine bottles are emptied into the sink.

halfGrip.analysis: The bottles were stored correctly, but nobody tasted them.
halfGrip.experience: Everyone got home, but the wine faded overnight.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: A glass goes out that tastes tired.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: The next evening three bottles are poured away.

success.outcome: The bottles stand in the wine fridge with a date and a cork, and the next evening they are sold by the glass.

staff.outcome: The bottles are left open on the counter overnight.

staffTexts.success: Per vacuum-seals the bottles and writes the date.
staffTexts.fail: The bottles are left open on the counter overnight.

vb27-allergireaktion.title: Allergic reaction
vb27-allergireaktion.body: {gäst} at table {bord} is scratching their throat and struggling to breathe after a few mouthfuls.

guestLine.a: The guest's friend: “She's allergic to nuts! She has a pen in her bag!”
guestLine.b: The guest, weakly: “It … feels thick in my throat.”

steps.question: What is a severe allergic reaction that affects breathing called?

a.label: Lactose intolerance
a.explanation: Lactose intolerance causes stomach problems, not breathlessness. It is not an allergy.

b.label: Anaphylaxis
b.explanation: Anaphylaxis is a severe allergic reaction that can affect breathing and blood pressure. It can become life-threatening within minutes.

c.label: Food poisoning
c.explanation: Food poisoning usually comes after hours and causes stomach problems. Breathlessness after a few mouthfuls points to an allergy.

fail.outcome: The staff think it will pass. The guest's breathing gets heavier while the party look on anxiously.

steps.clue: Analysis: Anaphylaxis can become life-threatening within minutes.

steps.question: What does the guest need?

a.label: Help now, and someone to stay with her
a.explanation: Minutes count, and she must not be left alone.

b.label: To be left in peace for a while
b.explanation: Someone who withdraws can get worse without anyone seeing.

c.label: For the party to look after her
c.explanation: They can help, but the responsibility to act lies with the restaurant.

fail.outcome: Nobody knows what went wrong. The kitchen carries on as if nothing happened.

steps.clue: Experience: The guest needs help now, and someone to stay.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Give her a glass of water, and wait and see.
a.explanation: Water doesn't help with anaphylaxis.

b.label: Give her an antihistamine tablet from the first-aid box.
b.explanation: A tablet acts too slowly in a severe reaction.

c.label: Take her away to the staff room, so that she can rest in peace for a while, out of everyone's sight.
c.explanation: It takes time, and nobody sees if she gets worse.

d.label: Call 112, help her use the adrenaline pen, stay with her, and ask the kitchen to keep the dish.
d.explanation: 112 and adrenaline are what count. Whoever stays sees if she gets worse, and what is kept on the plate shows the kitchen where the mistake was.

fail.outcome: The guest gets worse. The party call for help themselves.
fail.ongoing: The whole room is looking at the table where the guest is struggling to breathe.

success.outcome: The ambulance is on its way, the guest is breathing more calmly, and the kitchen knows what went wrong.

staff.outcome: They stand helpless until the guest's party calls 112.

staffTexts.success: Per calls 112 and stays with the guest.
staffTexts.fail: They stand helpless until the guest's party calls 112.

vb28-kylen-stannar.title: The fridge has stopped
vb28-kylen-stannar.body: In the middle of the evening: the fridge with the cheese and charcuterie has gone quiet. The thermometer shows 14 degrees.

guestLine.a: Sara: “The guests keep ordering the charcuterie board. What should I say?”
guestLine.b: The chef: “Should we throw everything out?”

steps.question: What decides whether cheese and charcuterie from a fridge that has stopped can be used?

a.label: As long as the product smells fine it is safe
a.explanation: Bacteria do not smell. Products that have been above 8 degrees for too long are a risk, whatever they smell like.

b.label: Everything in a fridge that has stopped must be thrown away
b.explanation: Safe, but more expensive than it needs to be. What has only been warm for a short time can be moved and saved.

c.label: How long the product has been warm and how warm it has got
c.explanation: When the fridge has stopped, the products must be judged by time and temperature. Whatever has been warm for too long is thrown away.

fail.outcome: The charcuterie goes out. Nobody notices anything tonight.
fail.ongoing: The charcuterie from the warm fridge goes out to the tables.

steps.clue: Analysis: Time and temperature in the food decide what can be saved.

steps.question: What does the evening need?

a.label: That everything is thrown out, to be on the safe side
a.explanation: Safe, but what has stayed cold can be saved.

b.label: That it is dealt with after service
b.explanation: By then the goods have been warm all evening.

c.label: That the floor knows where things stand before the guests order
c.explanation: A no before the order feels better than a no after.

fail.outcome: Guest after guest orders charcuterie that is not available. The waiters run between the kitchen and the tables.

steps.clue: Experience: The floor needs to know before the guests choose.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Measure in the food, move what's cold, discard the rest, tell the floor and log the deviation.
a.explanation: Measuring separates the safe from the unsafe, the floor can steer the guests, and the own-check log shows what happened.

b.label: Measure, move what's cold and discard the rest, but say nothing to the floor.
b.explanation: The goods are handled correctly, but guest after guest orders charcuterie that isn't there.

c.label: Tell the floor what's off, and pack everything into the other fridge.
c.explanation: Food that has been too warm shouldn't go in with the rest, and an overfull fridge cools worse.

d.label: Close the door, and wait for the fridge to start by itself.
d.explanation: Every minute in the warmth makes more of the food unsafe.

fail.outcome: The products are left in the warm fridge as time goes by.

success.outcome: The goods are sorted, the menu gets shorter, and the floor knows before the guests order.

staff.outcome: They keep serving from the warm fridge.

staffTexts.success: The chef measures, sorts and tells Sara.
staffTexts.fail: They keep serving from the warm fridge.

vb29-brak.title: Trouble at the bar
vb29-brak.body: The guest at the bar who has had a lot to drink starts arguing with a party next to them. Voices are raised.

guestLine.a: The guest, loudly, to the party next to them: “What are you staring at?”
guestLine.b: The guest, to the bartender: “Everyone's against me tonight.”

steps.question: What applies to serving a guest who is noticeably drunk?

a.label: The guest may be served if they eat something first
a.explanation: Food does not change the rule. Someone who is noticeably intoxicated must not be served alcohol.

b.label: It is the guest's own responsibility
b.explanation: The responsibility lies with whoever serves. It is in the Alcohol Act and in your alcohol licence.

c.label: Only spirits are forbidden to serve
c.explanation: The ban applies to all alcohol, wine and beer too.

d.label: The guest must not be served any more alcohol
d.explanation: The Alcohol Act forbids serving anyone who is noticeably intoxicated. It applies from the moment the staff see it.

fail.outcome: The bartender tops up the glass. The guest gets louder by the minute.

steps.clue: Analysis: No more alcohol for a noticeably intoxicated guest.

steps.question: What does the bar need?

a.label: Calm, and for the guest to leave without losing face
a.explanation: Calm and privacy dampen a quarrel. Humiliation sets it alight.

b.label: A telling-off the whole room can hear
b.explanation: A telling-off in public makes the quarrel bigger.

c.label: For the party to be moved to another table
c.explanation: It protects the party, but the guest is still there.

fail.outcome: The voices rise further. The party next to them leaves.
fail.ongoing: The voices at the bar are rising. Several tables ask for the bill.

steps.clue: Experience: The guest must not lose face.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Give one last drink, so that the guest calms down and leaves.
a.explanation: More alcohol doesn't calm a quarrel, and it isn't allowed.

b.label: Tell the guest loudly to calm down, so the whole room hears that you take it seriously.
b.explanation: The guest doesn't want to lose face, and the quarrel grows.

c.label: Put out water, talk calmly with the guest aside, and arrange a taxi.
c.explanation: Water and no alcohol are what the law requires. A calm talk and a taxi get the guest home safely.

d.label: Take the glass from the guest, and tell them to leave.
d.explanation: The right idea, but a glass taken out of your hand in front of others feels like humiliation.

fail.outcome: The guest raises their voice at the bartender too.
fail.ongoing: The voices at the bar get louder. The tables around are looking over.

halfGrip.analysis: The law was followed, but the guest was humiliated.
halfGrip.experience: The guest calmed down for a while, but the law was broken.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: The guest slaps the bar on the way out.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: A quarter of an hour later the voices rise again.

success.outcome: The guest goes outside with you. The taxi comes. The bar calms down.

staff.outcome: They stand behind the bar and wait. The party next to them leaves.

staffTexts.success: Elin puts out water and calls a taxi.
staffTexts.fail: They stand behind the bar and wait. The party next to them leaves.

vb30-korkgasten.title: The guest with the corked bottle
vb30-korkgasten.body: The guest who got the corked bottle earlier waves {personal} over and says loudly that the wine bar does not know its wine.

guestLine.a: The guest, loudly: “You don't even know your own wine!”
guestLine.b: The guest, audibly to the party: “This place has no idea.”

steps.question: What gives a wine a corked smell?

a.label: TCA, a compound that usually comes from the cork
a.explanation: TCA gives the smell of a damp cellar and wet cardboard. You cannot see it in the wine and you cannot air it away.

b.label: The wine has oxidised
b.explanation: Oxidation gives a tired, apple-like or nutty note. A corked smell is something else: a damp cellar.

c.label: Bits of cork that have got into the wine
c.explanation: Bits of cork are harmless and give no smell. They can be strained out; a corked smell cannot.

fail.outcome: {personal} says it is just a few bits of cork. The guest snorts.

steps.clue: Analysis: Cork taint (TCA) can't be aired away.

steps.question: What is the guest looking for?

a.label: For the mistake to be admitted, and put right so everyone sees it
a.explanation: The guest was right from the start and wants it to show.

b.label: To get the bottle for free
b.explanation: That may be part of it, but what the guest wants is to be put in the right.

c.label: An explanation that cork taint is always the producer's fault, not the bar's
c.explanation: Defending yourself makes the mistake bigger.

fail.outcome: The guest gets up, pays and leaves with their party.
fail.ongoing: The party leaves, and the other tables have heard what was said.

steps.clue: Experience: The guest wants to be put in the right.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Explain that cork taint is always the producer's fault and not the bar's, and that the bottle has to be paid for.
a.explanation: It is the wine bar that should have noticed the fault.

b.label: Admit the mistake, open a new bottle at the table, change the glasses and offer it on the house.
b.explanation: The guest sees the bottle is new, the glasses carry no cork taint, and a generous correction turns an unhappy guest into one who comes back.

c.label: Open a new bottle at the table and change the glasses, and charge as usual.
c.explanation: The exchange is right, but the mistake isn't admitted.

d.label: Admit the mistake and offer a new bottle on the house, opened at the bar.
d.explanation: The redress is right, but this guest needs to see the exchange.

fail.outcome: The new wine still smells faintly of cellar. The guest shakes their head.

halfGrip.analysis: The wine was put right, but the mistake was never admitted.
halfGrip.experience: The mistake was admitted, but the guest didn't see the exchange.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: The guest drinks in silence and pays early.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: The guest sniffs the new glass suspiciously.

success.outcome: A new bottle on the house. The guest raises a glass to the staff.

staff.outcome: They pretend not to hear. The guest pays and leaves with their party.

staffTexts.success: Elin admits the mistake and opens a new bottle at the table.
staffTexts.fail: They pretend not to hear. The guest pays and leaves with their party.

vb31-servetter-och-isen.title: The napkins and the ice
vb31-servetter-och-isen.body: It is {klockan}. Both the cloth napkins and the ice have run out, and {personal} only has time for one of them before the next wave of orders.

situations.middag: Tables are still being reset for dinner guests, and most people are ordering food.
situations.efter-middag: Dinner is over at most tables. The evening is moving towards drinks and avec.

guestLine.a: {personal}: “Ten tables need resetting for dinner, and we have no napkins.”
guestLine.b: {personal}: “Everyone wants drinks now, and the ice has run out.”

steps.question: What is an avec?

a.label: Spirits or liqueur with coffee after the meal
a.explanation: Avec is served with coffee when dinner is over, for example cognac or liqueur. When that time comes, the bar takes over the evening.

b.label: An aperitif before the meal
b.explanation: The aperitif comes before the meal and is meant to wake up the appetite. Avec comes after, with the coffee.

c.label: A glass of wine with the main course
c.explanation: The wine with the food is the meal drink. Avec is what is served with coffee afterwards.

fail.outcome: {personal} does not know what the guests will soon be ordering and stands still a moment too long.

steps.clue: Analysis: Avec comes with the coffee, after the meal.

steps.question: What does the evening need right now?

a.label: A bit of both, so that nobody goes completely without
a.explanation: Then nothing is ready when it's needed.

b.label: To wait until it has calmed down
b.explanation: Then both are missing just when the guests need them.

c.label: What the next wave of guests needs first
c.explanation: In a rush you choose what the evening needs now.

fail.outcome: Both the tables and the bar are without what they need when the wave comes.
fail.ongoing: The guests are waiting both for set tables and for their drinks.

steps.clue: Experience: Read what the next wave needs.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Scoop ice with a glass, it's quickest, and do the napkins later.
a.explanation: A glass can break in the ice, and a shard can't be seen among the cubes. Then the whole ice well has to be emptied.

b.label: Split the staff, one on the napkins and one on the ice.
b.explanation: Splitting means nothing is ready when it's needed.

c.label: Fold napkins for the tables first. The ice can wait.
c.explanation: At dinner the tables need setting. After dinner the evening turns to drinks, and then the bar stops without ice.

d.label: Fetch ice in a clean bucket with a scoop. The napkins can wait.
d.explanation: Ice is food. A scoop and a clean bucket keep it clean. After dinner it is the ice that's needed, at dinner the napkins.

fail.outcome: The ice well has to be emptied and refilled. The bar stands still while it is done.

halfGrip.analysis: The work was done right, but in the wrong order for the evening.
halfGrip.experience: The ice came quickly, but with a glass in the ice well.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: What was needed now is still waiting.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: The bartender looks down into the ice and hesitates.

success.outcome: What the evening needs is ready in time, and the orders go out at a steady pace.

staff.outcome: They do a bit of both, and the bar is without ice for a long while.
staff.ongoing: The ice has run out at the bar. The guests are waiting for their drinks.

staffTexts.success: {personal} takes what is needed first.
staffTexts.fail: They do a bit of both, and the bar is without ice for a long while.

vb32-fodelsedagen.title: The birthday
vb32-fodelsedagen.body: The host in lounge A waves discreetly to Per and whispers that it is Karin's birthday tonight. She knows nothing.

guestLine.a: The host whispers: “She knows nothing, and she loves to sing.” In lounge B two guests are deep in a business discussion.
guestLine.b: The host whispers: “We want to sing to her!” In lounge B a couple who have just got their main course talk quietly.

steps.question: Per is to order a dessert with candles. What does the kitchen need to know?

a.label: That candles and a lighter go on the tray
a.explanation: The candles are the floor's job. The kitchen needs to know what, how many and when.

b.label: How many it's for and when
b.explanation: Almost, but allergies come before everything, even at a party.

c.label: Numbers, allergies and when it goes out
c.explanation: The kitchen plans in numbers and time, and allergies come before everything.

d.label: Which dessert the host would prefer
d.explanation: The wish matters, but first the kitchen needs to know what is safe.

fail.outcome: I’ll take care of it.

steps.clue: Analysis: The kitchen needs more than an order.

steps.question: What does the evening need at the two tables?

a.label: A short party for Karin, and peace for the neighbours
a.explanation: The evening belongs to every table, and both can be given.

b.label: As much noise as possible, so the party shows
b.explanation: Then the neighbours can't hear their own conversation.

c.label: Karin celebrated, and the neighbours will have to put up with it
c.explanation: The neighbours are guests of the evening too.

fail.outcome: I’ll take care of it.
fail.ongoing: I’ll take care of it.

steps.clue: Experience: Two tables want different things from the evening.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Give the kitchen everything it needs, and ask the party to hold off on the song.
a.explanation: The kitchen gets the right word, but the neighbours may sit for a long time, and then there is no song for Karin.

b.label: Give the kitchen everything, one verse for Karin, a glass for the neighbours.
b.explanation: A short party and a gesture to the neighbours. It costs, but both tables remember the evening.
b.success: One verse for Karin. In lounge B the neighbours raise their glasses to her.

c.label: Give the kitchen everything, one verse for Karin, apologise to the neighbours first.
c.explanation: The neighbours know what's coming and feel seen. It is cheaper, but the gesture is smaller.
c.success: One verse for Karin. The neighbours smile and carry on their conversation.

d.label: A verse, something for the neighbours, and the cake out without asking about allergies.
d.explanation: Both tables get theirs, but nobody asked about allergies.

fail.outcome: I’ll take care of it.

halfGrip.analysis: The kitchen got everything it needed, but Karin got no song.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: The cake arrives in silence. The host looks disappointed.
halfGrip.experience: Both tables got theirs, but nobody asked about allergies before the cake went out.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: One guest in the party doesn't eat the cake.

success.outcome: One verse for Karin. In lounge B the neighbours raise their glasses to her.

staff.outcome: Per takes over. The cake goes out, but nobody has asked about allergies.

staffTexts.success: Per asks about allergies and asks the party to sing one verse.
staffTexts.fail: Per takes over. The cake goes out, but nobody has asked about allergies.

vb33-vasen.title: The vase on the desk
vb33-vasen.body: A guest in a wheelchair comes in between the host’s desk and the coat rail. A hand on the wheel catches the desk, and the vase smashes on the floor.

guestLine.a: The guest, red in the face: “Sorry, sorry! I'll pay for the vase.”
guestLine.b: The guest's companion: “This happens everywhere. Maybe we should go home.”

steps.question: What is the risk right now?

a.label: That the guest has hurt a hand on the desk
a.explanation: You ask about that in the next step. Right now the glass and the water are a risk to everyone in the entrance.

b.label: That the entrance is blocked for the next party
b.explanation: The queue can wait a minute. Shards in the entrance can't.

c.label: Broken glass and water where guests walk in
c.explanation: Glass and water in the entrance are a risk to everyone coming in, wheelchair wheels too.

d.label: That the water ruins the booking book on the desk
d.explanation: The book can be dried. Shards are a risk to people.

fail.outcome: Nobody does anything. The glass lies where the next guest will come in.

steps.clue: Analysis: Shards and water in the entrance are a risk to everyone.

steps.question: What does the guest need?

a.label: To hear it wasn't their fault, and to feel welcome
a.explanation: The entrance was too narrow for a wheelchair. The mistake is the restaurant's.

b.label: To pay for the vase
b.explanation: Taking money confirms that the mistake was the guest's.

c.label: An apology and a glass on the house
c.explanation: Generous, but without an explanation the guest may think you are treating them because they did wrong.

fail.outcome: The guest sits in silence and looks down at the table.
fail.ongoing: The guest in the wheelchair sits in silence at their table.

steps.clue: Experience: The guest is ashamed, though the mistake was the restaurant's.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Say the mistake was ours and offer the evening on the house, and clean up after them.
a.explanation: The words are right, but the guests roll and walk through the glass before it is swept.

b.label: Pick up the big shards by hand, and say it could happen to anyone.
b.explanation: Hands get cut on shards, and the blame is put on the guest.

c.label: Ask how the guest is, sweep up, say the mistake was ours and move the stand.
c.explanation: The person first, then the risk, then the cause. The stand was in the way, and now it isn't.

d.label: Cordon off, sweep and mop, and then show the way to the table.
d.explanation: The cleaning is right, but nobody says the mistake was the restaurant's, and the guest stays ashamed.

fail.outcome: The shards are still in the entrance, and the guest thinks the mistake was theirs.

halfGrip.analysis: The entrance was cleaned, but the guest had to carry the blame.
halfGrip.experience: The guest felt welcome, but the glass lay there too long.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: The guest sits in silence for the rest of the evening.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: The wheel crunches over a shard.

success.outcome: The entrance is clear. The stand is now where a wheelchair can get past, and the guest is at their table.

staff.outcome: Per sweeps up, but nobody moves the stand.

staffTexts.success: Per asks how the guest is, sweeps up and moves the stand.
staffTexts.fail: Per sweeps up, but nobody moves the stand.

vb34-vinglar.title: The unsteady guest
vb34-vinglar.body: A guest slides off his bar stool, takes one step too far back and walks straight into Sara’s tray.

guestLine.a: The friends: “Come on, we're regulars. We'll order for him.”
guestLine.b: The guest, embarrassed: “Sorry, Sara. I just tripped.”

steps.question: What does the Alcohol Act say about a guest who is noticeably intoxicated?

a.label: He may be served if he eats something first
a.explanation: Food doesn't change the rule. Someone who is noticeably intoxicated must not be served.

b.label: He may be served beer, but not spirits
b.explanation: The ban covers all alcohol, beer and wine too.

c.label: He must leave the premises at once
c.explanation: The law forbids serving, not staying. Whether he may stay is up to you, depending on how he is.

d.label: He may not be served any more alcohol
d.explanation: Someone who is noticeably intoxicated must not be served alcohol, whatever the drink.

fail.outcome: Mira pours without thinking.

steps.clue: Analysis: No more alcohol for him.

steps.question: What does the guest need?

a.label: To be asked to leave
a.explanation: It may become necessary, but he has done nothing more than trip.

b.label: To get out of this without being shamed in front of his friends
b.explanation: A no given calmly and in private is taken better.

c.label: To carry on the evening as usual
c.explanation: That can't happen, and he probably knows it himself.

fail.outcome: The friends laugh, and he orders another.
fail.ongoing: The friends at the bar order for him.

steps.clue: Experience: He is ashamed, and his friends want to help in the wrong way.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Say no to him and his friends loudly at the bar, and then note the time.
a.explanation: The law is followed, but he is humiliated in front of his friends.

b.label: Let the friends order, but ask them not to give him anything.
b.explanation: Kind, but if the glass is passed on to him you have served him.

c.label: Let them order, he has only had water after all.
c.explanation: The ban applies whoever does the ordering.

d.label: Calmly refuse more alcohol, give water and food, and note the time.
d.explanation: A calm no protects him, water and food show care, and the time on the note shows you did right.

fail.outcome: The glasses are passed on to him, and he gets louder at the bar.

halfGrip.analysis: The law was followed, but he was ashamed in front of his friends.
halfGrip.experience: The mood held, but a glass was passed on to him.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: The party pays and leaves in silence.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: He drinks from his friend's glass.

success.outcome: He drinks water and eats. Mira writes: refused {klockan}.

staff.outcome: Mira lets the friends order. The glasses are passed on to him.

staffTexts.success: Mira calmly says no and puts out water.
staffTexts.fail: Mira lets the friends order. The glasses are passed on to him.

vb36-passet.title: The guest at the pass
vb36-passet.body: A guest gets up from lounge A and heads straight for the kitchen. At the hatch she asks if she may look inside.

guestLine.a: The guest: “I've always wondered what it looks like behind the hatch. Just a quick look?”
guestLine.b: The guest: “I write about food for Grythyttebladet. May I see how you work?”

steps.question: What applies when a guest wants to go into a restaurant kitchen?

a.label: That she touches nothing and stays by the door
a.explanation: That isn't enough. Anyone who goes into the kitchen follows the same hygiene rules as the staff.

b.label: Protective clothing, hand-washing and an escort
b.explanation: The kitchen is a food premises. Anyone going in must wear protective clothing, wash their hands and be accompanied.

c.label: That she isn’t ill; the chef answers for the rest
c.explanation: Health is part of it, but clothing, hand-washing and company are needed too.

d.label: That it’s only allowed when nothing is being cooked
d.explanation: It's a sensible time, but not a rule. The rules apply whatever the time.

fail.outcome: She stays at the pass, waiting for an answer.

steps.clue: Analysis: The kitchen is a food premises with the same rules for everyone.

steps.question: What is the guest looking for?

a.label: Special treatment
a.explanation: She asked for a look, not for favours.

b.label: A short look, as quickly as possible, while the kitchen works
b.explanation: It's what she asked for, but a kitchen in a rush doesn't show itself in a second.

c.label: To see how the kitchen really works
c.explanation: Curiosity is a gift. It is possible to give her something without breaking the rules.

fail.outcome: She goes back to her table without an answer.
fail.ongoing: The guest keeps looking towards the pass.

steps.clue: Experience: The guest is curious about the craft.

steps.question: What do you do?

a.label: Give her an apron and a look from the door, and offer a tour after service.
a.explanation: The rules are followed, the kitchen isn't disturbed, and the curiosity gets a real answer.

b.label: Say kindly that the kitchen doesn't take guests during service.
b.explanation: Safe, but she asked for something you can give.

c.label: Take her straight in and show all the stations while you cook.
c.explanation: Generous, but without protective clothing and in the middle of the rush.

d.label: Ask Elin to take special care of her for the rest of the evening, so she feels special.
d.explanation: The same rules for everyone. What you can give extra is time, when the kitchen has time.

fail.outcome: The guest stays at the pass while the kitchen works around her.

halfGrip.analysis: The rules were followed, but she got nothing.
halfGrip.experience: She got to see everything, but without protective clothing in the full rush.
halfGrip.outcomeAnalysis: She looks towards the hatch for the rest of the evening.
halfGrip.outcomeExperience: A plate has to wait while the chef shows her round.

success.outcome: A tour after service? I'd love to!

staff.outcome: Nobody answers her. She goes back to her table.

staffTexts.success: The chef gives her an apron and a look from the door.
staffTexts.fail: Nobody answers her. She goes back to her table.

vb35-tillsynen-a.title: The inspection
vb35-tillsynen-a.body: Two guests at the high table haven’t touched their glasses for a while. Now they each show Per an ID card.

guestLine.a: The case officer: “We're from the municipality. Carry on as usual, we're just looking.”
guestLine.b: The police officer: “Routine check. Who is responsible tonight?”

steps.question: Who must be on the premises throughout serving hours?

a.label: Someone who has done the responsible alcohol serving course
a.explanation: The course is good, but not enough. The name must be registered with the municipality.

b.label: The bartender, since she is the one pouring
b.explanation: The one pouring doesn't have to be responsible. The responsibility lies with the person who is registered.

c.label: The licence holder or a registered serving supervisor
c.explanation: One of them must be on site throughout the serving hours.

d.label: The owner in person, every evening serving is on
d.explanation: The owner can register others. It is enough for one of them to be on site.

fail.outcome: Nobody knows who is responsible tonight. Per looks around.

steps.clue: Analysis: A registered responsible person must be on site all evening.

steps.question: What is the inspection looking for?

a.label: To see how you work on an ordinary evening
a.explanation: The inspection wants to see everyday work, not a show.

b.label: To find faults they can remark on in the report
b.explanation: They aren't looking for faults, they're checking that the routines hold.

c.label: To see the papers as quickly as possible
c.explanation: The papers are needed, but it's the work they want to see.

vb40-karaffen.title: The decanter
vb40-karaffen.body: {gäst} at table {bord} orders an older Barolo, the 2008 vintage. When {personal} tilts the bottle towards the light, there is sediment.

guestLine.a: “We bought this when our daughter was born. We've kept it for fifteen years.”
guestLine.b: “This is our wedding vintage. We were married fifteen years ago today.”

steps.question: Why do you decant an older wine?

a.label: To air it, like a young wine
a.explanation: An older wine is fragile and can lose its nose from too much air.

b.label: To separate the wine from the sediment
b.explanation: The sediment is old pigments and tannins that have dropped out. It tastes bitter and clouds the glass.

c.label: To warm the wine to the right temperature
c.explanation: The decanter does not change the temperature noticeably.

d.label: Because it looks nice at the table
d.explanation: It does, but decanting has a purpose.

fail.outcome: {personal} opens the bottle like a young wine. The sediment stirs in the bottle.

steps.clue: Analysis: The bottle has sediment, and the wine is fragile.

steps.question: What are the guests looking for?

a.label: For the wine to be served quickly
a.explanation: They have waited fifteen years. Tonight it is not speed that counts.

b.label: For the bottle to be treated as the memory it is
b.explanation: How the bottle is opened is part of the evening.

c.label: An explanation of how Barolo ages in the bottle over the years
c.explanation: It might be fun, but the guests spoke about their memory, not about the grape.

fail.outcome: The bottle is opened quickly and without a word. The guests look at each other.

steps.clue: Experience: The bottle is a memory.

steps.question: Put the cards in the order you would do it. You don't have to use them all.

full.label: Full grip
full.explanation: The candle shows when the sediment is coming, and slow pouring protects a fragile wine. Doing it at the table makes the opening part of the memory.

analysis.label: Half grip: the analysis held
analysis.explanation: The technique was right, but the guests were not there when their bottle was opened.

experience.label: Half grip: the experience held
experience.explanation: The care was right, but too much air and waiting take the nose from an older wine.

wrong.label: Wrong
wrong.explanation: Neither the wine nor the guests’ evening held this time. The bottle is shown at the table, the candle is lit, and the sediment stays in the bottle.

fail.outcome: The wine is poured straight from the bottle. The bottoms of the glasses turn cloudy.
